'''Donald MacCrimmon MacKay''' (9 August 1922 – 6 February 1987) was a British [[physicist]], and professor at the Department of Communication and Neuroscience at [[Keele University]] in Staffordshire, England, known for his contributions to [[information theory]] and the theory of brain organisation.<ref>[http://www.giffordlectures.org/lecturers/donald-maccrimmon-mackay Donald MacCrimmon MacKay] Gifford Lectures bio</ref>

==Education==
MacKay was educated at [[Wick High School]] and [[St Andrews University]], and gained a PhD at [[King's College London]].<ref>{{cite thesis|last=MacKay|first=D. M.|title=The application of electronic principles to the solution of differential equations in physics.|year=1951|institution=[[King's College London|University of London (King's College)]]|url=https://librarysearch.kcl.ac.uk:443/kings_v1:EVERYTHING:44KCL_ALEPH_DS001581352|at=[[Maughan Library]]: Index to theses, 2-2818|id=Barcode 0202950465}}</ref> In the late 1940s MacKay was among the first members of the [[Ratio Club]].

==Personal life==
Married to Valerie Wood, they had five children.  His oldest son is [[Robert Sinclair MacKay]], a professor of mathematics at the [[University of Warwick]]; his youngest son was [[David J. C. MacKay]], a professor of physics at the [[University of Cambridge]]. He died within a year of giving the 1986 [[Gifford Lectures]] at the [[University of Glasgow]].

== Quotes ==
<blockquote> In our age, when people look for explanations, the tendency more and more is to conceive of any and every situation that we are trying to understand by analogy with a machine.<ref>Cited in: [[Sytse Strijbos]] (1988) ''Het Technische Wereldbeeld''. p. 13.</ref></blockquote>

<blockquote>God's way of working has been slow and gradual (the bodies of higher animals coming into being through descent with modification from earlier species), is all that is meant by the term 'evolution' as used in science. In this technical, scientific sense the idea is theologically neutral, and is widely accepted by biologists who are also biblical Christians. Nothing in the Bible rules it out.<ref>Mackay, Donald M. (1997 edition). ''Clockwork Image: Christian Perspective on Science''. Inter-Varsity Press. p. 51. {{ISBN|978-0851112428}}</ref></blockquote>

==Selected publications==
MacKay authored several publications. A selection:
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon, [http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v159/n4038/abs/159406a0.html A high-speed electronic function generator], ''Nature'' '''159''' (4038): 406–407. 1947
* Deeley, E. M., MacKay, D. M., [http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v163/n4147/abs/163650a0.html Multiplication and division by electronic analogue methods], ''Nature'' '''163''' (4147): 650-650. 1949
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon, [https://www.nature.com/articles/181362c0 Moving visual images produced by regular stationary pattern], ''Nature'' '''180''' : 849–850. 1957
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon, [http://mind.oxfordjournals.org/content/LXIX/273/31.extract III. On the logical indeterminacy of a free choice.]{{dead link|date=January 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}, ''Mind'', LXIX(273):31-40, 01 1960.
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon, [https://www.nature.com/articles/192739a0 Visual effects of non-redundant stimulation], ''Nature'' '''192''' (4804): 739–740. 1961
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon, and Michael Ellis Fisher. ''Analogue Computing at Ultra-High Speed: An Experimental and Theoretical Study''. London: Chapman & Hall, 1962.
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon. ''[https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/information-mechanism-and-meaning Information, Mechanism, and Meaning]''. Cambridge: MIT Press. 1970.
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon. ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=t8wqAQAAMAAJ The Clockwork Image: A Christian Perspective on Science]'' InterVarsity Press.  1974.
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon. ''Brains, Machines, and Persons''. Collins, 1980.
* MacKay, Donald MacCrimmon, and Valerie Mackay (ed). ''Behind the Eye''. Basil Blackwell, 1991.
